title: Trapezoid midsegment, base angles and diagonals

beats.say: This orchard ladder narrows as it climbs.
The bottom rung is twenty-four inches. The top rung, twelve.
How long is the rung exactly halfway up?
Each rung is three inches shorter than the last, so the middle one is eighteen: halfway between. That's the average. Add the two, divide by two.
The ladder's outline is a trapezoid: four straight sides, with exactly one pair parallel, pointing the same way, never meeting.
Those two are the bases. The other two are the legs.
Name the corners in order around the shape: A, B, C, D. So A B and D C are the bases.
A bar over the letters means the side itself, and this symbol means parallel.
Join the midpoints of the legs, the points halfway along them, M and N.
That's the midsegment, the middle rung, and its length is always the average of the bases.
Slide the top base sideways. The midsegment keeps its length.
Here's why. Give an identical copy a half turn about the midpoint of a leg.
The two pieces lock into a parallelogram.
Its long side is one base plus the other.
And straight across the middle, two midsegments make that same length.
So one midsegment is the sum of the bases, divided by two.
Try one. A B is x plus six. D C is three x plus eight. The midsegment is twenty-five. Find A B.

do.text: In trapezoid $ABCD$, $AB = x+6$, $DC = 3x+8$, and the midsegment is $25$. Find $AB$.

beats.say: Write the average.
On top, x and three x make four x, and six and eight make fourteen.
Multiply both sides by two to clear the fraction.
Subtract fourteen.
Divide by four.
x is nine.
But they asked for A B, not x. Nine plus six: fifteen.
Check: D C is thirty-five, and the average of fifteen and thirty-five is twenty-five.
If a base is the unknown, it's the same equation: double the midsegment, then subtract the base you know.
Now make the legs equal, shown by these tick marks, or this symbol. That's an isosceles trapezoid.

do.text: Isosceles: the legs are the same length.

beats.say: Flip it over its mirror line, and it lands exactly on its own outline.
A and B trade places, and so do C and D. So the two angles on the same base are equal.
Flip it back, and watch the diagonals, the lines joining opposite corners. They trade places too, so they're equal.
The measure of an angle is its size in degrees. Angle D is three x plus ten, and angle C is five x minus thirty. Same base, so set them equal.
Collect the x terms on one side, the numbers on the other. Two x is forty, so x is twenty.
Angle C is seventy degrees.
Diagonals work the same way. A C is four x minus five, and B D is x plus four. Set them equal: x is three, so A C is seven.
One more, for every trapezoid.
Slide angle D up the leg. The bases are parallel, so its size doesn't change.
At the top it sits beside angle A, and together they fill a straight line: one hundred eighty degrees.
So if angle D is fifty-seven, angle A is one hundred twenty-three.
The midsegment also gives you area. Cut off each corner, and give it a half turn about a midpoint.
Now it's a rectangle, as wide as the midsegment. So area is midsegment times height.
The same idea works for anything that changes steadily.
A train slows steadily from sixty miles an hour to forty, over two hours.
Its average speed is the midsegment: fifty.
Fifty miles an hour for two hours is a hundred miles: the area of this trapezoid.

do.text: miles, the area under the line

beats.say: Slice a curve into thin trapezoids, and the same calculation closes in on the area beneath it.
That's the doorway to calculus.
Midsegment: average the bases.
Isosceles: same-base angles are equal, and so are the diagonals.
Same-leg angles always add to one hundred eighty.
Set up the equation, solve for x, and answer what they asked.
